author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Rez: synchronizing lock-on shooting, generative music and vibration into one PS2 pulse
summary: United Game Artists designed every shot as an audiovisual event quantized into the music, then extended the rhythm through DualShock vibration and the unusual Trance Vibrator peripheral.

sourceLabels.postmortem: Tetsuya Mizuguchi Takes a Postmortem Look at the Making of Rez

blocks.text: The player adds events to an existing track

Rez is a rail shooter, but firing does not sit independently over background music. Locking targets, releasing shots, destroying enemies and collecting items trigger sounds placed within the track's rhythmic structure. The player does not compose freely; they perform inside a authored musical framework whose feedback always tries to sound intentional.
Lock-on separates aiming from musical release

Holding the button can mark several targets before release. This gives time to scan the visual field and lets one action produce a phrase rather than a stream of unrelated shots. Choosing when to release balances danger, score and musical satisfaction. The system makes rhythm accessible without requiring every player to press on an exact beat.

Triggered sounds align to musical timing so imperfect input does not create a chaotic mix. That processing is central to the promise that ordinary play produces coherent audio. Too much correction could make timing meaningless; too little would punish the intended free shooting. Rez positions player agency in target selection and phrase density while the engine preserves musical structure.
Wireframes leave room for sound and transformation

Sparse polygonal forms, luminous particles and evolving avatars avoid realistic visual noise. Enemies and environments pulse, unfold and accumulate detail as the track develops. The abstraction supports technical performance and the fictional journey through a network, but more importantly it gives each hit a clear visual counterpart to its sound.
Levels are arrangements, not only routes

Enemy waves, camera movement, background layers and boss phases follow the arc of each composition. Intensity rises through both denser hazards and richer audio. A level designer must therefore coordinate challenge with musical development; a mechanically reasonable wave placed at the wrong phrase can break the sensation of one continuous performance.
Vibration extended rhythm beyond the screen

DualShock feedback pulses with events, and the Japanese PS2 release supported a dedicated USB Trance Vibrator designed to be placed against the body. The accessory did not provide directional control. It made low-frequency timing physical, treating touch as another output channel alongside line, color and sound.
Minimalism still depends on exact synchronization

A small audio delay, irregular frame time or missing vibration can damage Rez more than a modest resolution error. The image is intentionally simple enough that temporal relationships become exposed. Music streaming, shot samples, animation and haptics must stay aligned over an entire area, including transitions where layers enter or leave.
Emulation should test the complete sensory chain

Tests need wired audio where possible, stable frame pacing, correct USB peripheral behavior and controller rumble. Upscaling should preserve thin lines without creating shimmering or making particle bloom harsh. Input latency measurements should include the delay from button release to quantized sound, distinguishing intentional musical alignment from emulator buffering.

Rez does not merely place electronic music behind a shooter. It distributes one rhythm across aiming, release, sound, image and touch. Every subsystem accepts some constraint so their outputs can agree. That coordination made an abstract, short game historically durable: players remember not a single mechanic or song, but the sensation that several senses were being edited by the same pulse.
